To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
mouse embryos can survive direct transfer to -196°C after rapid cooling in DMSO and that survival depends on the temperature at which cooling is terminated.

mouse embryos survive freezing at -196 degrees C after slow cooling (0.3-0.6 degrees/min) in 0.5 M or 1.5 DMSO to temperatures of -10 to -40 degrees C followed by direct transfer to liquid N2 (-196 degrees C) and rapid warming (275-500 degrees/min) to room temperature, and that survival is similar to that after conventional slow thawing at 0 degrees/min.

mouse embryos can be rapidly frozen and thawed with good survival, but the embryos need to be cooled slowly to a high subzero temperature (-35 degrees C) before rapid transfer to -196 degree C, and that embryos can be thawed rapidly at room temperature without loss of viability.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of cryoprotective agents on the survival and development of embryos.
the development and application of methods for the cryopreservation of mammalian embryos.
the survival of frozen mouse embryos.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the survival rate of frozen-thawed mouse embryos is dependent on the temperature to which the samples are cooled prior to storage and the rate at which the samples are thawed.
(a) mouse embryos are not particularly sensitive to the stresses of cryopreservation; and (b) a simple and rapid freezing procedure is adequate for the preservation of 8-cell embryos.
the rate of warming from liquid nitrogen is not a critical factor in the survival of frozen embryos.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a new method for the preservation and transport of mammalian embryos.
mouse embryos survive the freezing and thawing process if cooled rapidly and thawed rapidly.

the survival of mouse embryos frozen in 1. 5 M-DMS0 is similar to that in 0.5 M-DMSo, that the survival of 4-cell and 8-cell embryos is similar to that after blastocyst formation and that the survival of embryos frozen at -35 degrees C or below is similar to that frozen at -80 degrees C.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have shown that the rate of warming of embryos is critical to their survival.
the rate of warming from liquid nitrogen is critical for the survival of frozen embryos, and the optimal rate of warming for mouse embryos is 275-500 degrees C/min.
the freezing and thawing protocol is not the limiting step to survival of embryos.
